topics.question: What is debt recycling?
topics.prose:
Debt recycling is using your home loan as a tool to build an investment portfolio. You pay down some of your non‑deductible mortgage, then borrow that same amount in a separate loan and invest it, so the interest on that new loan is for investment and may be tax deductible.

In practice, it’s a simple loop. Make a lump sum payment on your home loan, set up a split or use a redraw, borrow back the same amount, and put it into income‑producing assets. On Equity Mates, this is described as turning home debt that gets you no tax break into investment debt that can be deducted because it funds investments, not your house. Some investors then use dividends or distributions plus their regular savings to reduce the home loan again, and repeat the cycle.

The bit people often get wrong is thinking it always means more debt. If you pay down and then reborrow the same amount, your total debt and repayments can stay the same, you’ve just changed the purpose of part of the debt, which is what makes the interest deductible. The extra risk shows up if you add new borrowings on top of what you already owe to invest more, which is still debt recycling but clearly increases your exposure to markets.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is that debt recycling is about tax treatment, not picking hot stocks. If your cash flow and total debt don’t change, the market risk you’re taking is similar to what you’d face investing that cash anyway, the difference is the interest may be deductible because of how the loan is structured. It’s also an ongoing process, not a one‑off set‑and‑forget, and an adviser on Equity Mates warned that doing it sloppily can make it inefficient.

The catch is that markets move, and borrowed money magnifies those moves. There’s also a quirky reality of our system, home loan interest isn’t deductible but investment loan interest is, which is why the structure matters. And while the aim is a tax deduction, Equity Mates has shown scenarios where the strategy actually leads to more tax paid over time because the investment income grows so large, even though net assets can end up higher as a result. Whether it suits any individual depends on their circumstances and is a question for a licensed adviser.

topics.question: What is an ETF?
topics.prose:
An ETF is a ready‑made bundle of investments you buy on the ASX like a normal share. Most aim to track a market index, so you get the index’s return, minus fees, without having to pick individual stocks yourself.

Here’s how it works in practice. You open a brokerage account, place one trade, and you own a slice of a whole basket, like the top 200 Aussie companies, rather than just one name. Because it trades on the exchange, you can buy or sell during market hours and there generally aren’t fund minimums beyond your broker’s rules, which is why ETFs are often described as easy to access and usually lower cost than old‑school managed funds.

The bit people mix up is ETF versus index fund. Both can aim to track the same index, but an ETF trades on the exchange while a traditional index fund is bought directly from the fund manager, with more admin and typically higher costs called out in the show’s basics episodes. And not all ETFs are the same, they are a wrapper over whatever’s inside, from broad markets to specific themes, so the basket changes with the strategy.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is read the name, it tells you a lot. The issuer, the market or region, the asset class, and whether it is index tracking or doing something more active are often right there, and the more complex the ETF, the more that naming matters. Then go to the issuer’s website for the purpose, holdings and fees, which they are required to publish clearly.

The catch is that easy does not mean effortless. ETFs are usually diversified compared to a single share, but they still reflect whatever market or theme they track, and costs still apply even when they are low. With so many choices, it can feel like stock picking again, which is why Equity Mates stresses understanding what is in the basket before you hit buy.

topics.question: What is dollar cost averaging?
topics.prose:
Dollar cost averaging is just setting up a habit to invest the same dollar amount on a regular timetable. When prices are up that cash buys fewer units, when prices are down it buys more, so your entry price gets smoothed and you stop stressing about timing every buy.

In practice it is simple. Pick a cadence that fits how you get paid, and automate the transfer so you invest the same amount each time. There is no rule on weekly vs monthly, but keep an eye on brokerage because lots of small trades can add up in costs.

The bit people get wrong is waiting for the perfect moment. On Equity Mates we keep saying it is nearly impossible to pick the top or the bottom, and dollar cost averaging takes that decision off your plate when markets are choppy or falling. You do not know when a fall will stop, which is exactly why some investors keep their plan going rather than trying to outguess the next move.

We also come back to behaviour. Automating a regular buy helps take the emotion out, which many listeners tell us simply makes it easier to stick with their plan. And you have probably been doing a version of it already without noticing, because superannuation contributions go in at a steady clip, no matter what markets are doing.

The main catch is that dollar cost averaging is not magic. In a falling market you can still be down for a while, even though the buys are smoothing the ride, as we have shown with real world examples on the show. And if you are buying individual companies rather than a broad basket, there is more risk because you are not diversified, which is why some investors prefer to use a DCA plan on diversified exposures instead of single stocks.

One more nuance we have discussed: in plenty of periods, lump sum investing has beaten spacing the same money out over time. Research we have covered found lump sums often win over a 12 month window, which is useful context for anyone weighing up the trade off between maths and mindset. Dollar cost averaging’s power is the habit and the headspace it gives you to keep going.

topics.question: What is compound interest?
topics.prose:
Compound interest is your money earning interest on the interest it already earned, so the pile grows on a bigger base each year. Think snowball, not straight line, which is why time is such a big deal for it to work well.

Here is the gist. Simple interest pays only on what you first put in. Compound interest pays on that original amount plus all the interest you have already earned, so the calculation steps up each year as the balance gets bigger.

A common mix‑up is thinking compounding only happens when you get paid interest or dividends in cash. On Equity Mates we explain it can also come from your investment price growing and then growing again off that higher base, though reinvesting any dividends helps and spending them stops the compounding effect in its tracks.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is time in the market. The effect is small at first then it accelerates, which is why starting early and letting returns build on themselves is such a powerful idea, even if you are adding modest amounts along the way. Markets jump around year to year, but the driver of compounding is staying invested so the base you are growing from can keep getting bigger over the long run.

The catch is patience and consistency. Compounding does not rescue a bad investment and it assumes the underlying asset keeps creating value over time, so the growth you are compounding actually shows up. Also, markets will be volatile, some years up and some down, so the magic is not instant and there are no guarantees about timing or outcomes, only the maths of returns building on a bigger base when they do arrive.

topics.prose:
Super is your long term retirement money. Your employer puts a slice of your pay into a fund, it’s invested, and the tax is lighter than your normal income, which is why on Equity Mates we call super the biggest free kick in finance. Pay attention to it, because that money compounds for decades whether you’re watching or not.

Here’s the gist. By law, your employer chips in to your super account, and that money is invested for you over time. You can also add more yourself before tax (concessional) or after tax (non concessional); for most people, before tax contributions are taxed at 15 percent rather than your marginal rate, and you can do it by salary sacrifice or even BPAY then claim a deduction at tax time. Equity Mates has also explained that concessional contributions are taxed at 15 percent provided your income is under $250k.

The part people get wrong is ignoring it. After a few jobs, it’s easy to end up with a handful of default funds, paying duplicate fees and insurance and watching small balances get eaten away; on Equity Mates we’ve talked through using myGov with the ATO to find what’s in your name and consolidate to one account to avoid paying for the same thing twice.

What we keep coming back to is engagement. Super is basically forced dollar cost averaging, with money going in every pay cycle, so check where it’s invested, what the fees are and how performance looks after fees; it’s the only free kick you get, so make sure the environment is doing its job. Super is the foundation of retirement in Australia, and even small tweaks here can make a meaningful difference over time.

The catch is access. Money in super is locked until a preservation age, and on Equity Mates we’ve spoken about it being in the 55 to 60 range and that governments tend to move it higher rather than lower, so super suits long term goals but trades off flexibility. From 60, a transition to retirement strategy can let you draw a limited amount while still working, which we’ve covered with an adviser on Equity Mates.

Rules can change. We’ve discussed proposals to tax earnings on very large balances more heavily, a good reminder to stay engaged and not set and forget your super setup.

topics.question: What are franking credits?
topics.prose:
Franking credits are the tax credits that often come attached to Australian dividends. They exist to stop you being taxed twice on the same company profits, and you use them at tax time to offset what you owe, or if you are on a lower tax rate, sometimes get some back as a refund. Equity Mates has covered this a lot because it is a very Aussie quirk of investing. 

Here is how it works in practice. A company pays tax on its profits, then pays you a dividend as cash plus a credit for the tax it already paid on that dividend. On your tax return you include the grossed up dividend as income, and the franking credit sits alongside it as a tax offset to reduce the bill. 

The bit people often get wrong is thinking it is free money. It is not, it is a credit for tax already paid, which means if your marginal tax rate is below the company tax that was paid, you can get a refund, and if your rate is higher, you pay a top up. You will see whether a dividend is franked on the dividend statement or the ASX page, and at tax time your dividend and franking data generally flows into the ATO prefill, which makes the admin a lot easier. 

Equity Mates keeps coming back to the simple idea behind it, franking is about avoiding double taxation. In Australia you can claim the credit back at the tax office because the company has already been taxed on those profits, which is why franking is such a feature of Aussie dividend investing. Only a small handful of countries run dividend imputation like this, and Australia is one of them. 

The main catches are straightforward. If your tax rate is higher than the company tax attached to the dividend, you still owe top up tax, and not every dividend is fully franked, so check the statement and remember final amounts settle at year end. The rules have also been politically debated in recent years, including a push to stop cash refunds for excess credits, which shows policy can change.

topics.question: What is an index fund?
topics.prose:
An index fund is a simple way to own a slice of a whole market in one go. It bundles a bunch of companies, like the top 200 on the ASX, and aims to match how that market moves, up or down.

Here is how it works. A market index takes a set of companies and tracks them over time, usually ranked from biggest to smallest, with no one hand picking winners or dumping losers along the way. An index fund is the vehicle that lets you invest in that index, so instead of choosing single stocks, you own a little bit of every company in the index.

The bit people get wrong is mixing up the index with the ETF. The index is what you invest in, the basket itself, while an ETF is just one way to access it on the stock exchange, and ETFs can also hold other strategies that are not indexes. Traditional index funds can be unlisted and handled directly with the fund manager, whereas an index ETF is listed and trades like a share during the day.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is the simplicity. All roads lead back to the index because the core idea is owning the market rather than trying to outsmart it, a shift that took off in the 1970s with the idea of just buying a bit of everything. The appeal we talk about a lot is broad diversification in one trade and, compared to many traditional actively managed funds, generally lower costs and easier access.

The catch is you get the market return, for better and for worse. If the market falls, your index fund falls with it, and you are not cherry picking which companies to own because the index holds them based on size and keeps tracking them regardless of how they are doing. Also, not every ETF is an index fund, so always check what the product is tracking, and many will say the index name in the title to make that clearer.

topics.question: What is diversification?
topics.prose:
Diversification is spreading your bets so one bad day does not sink your whole pile. It means owning a mix of things that do not all move together, so one wobble does not wipe you out and you can stay in the game longer.

In practice, it is mixing different types of assets and different places. On Equity Mates we talk about combining shares with other assets, and spreading across Australia, the US and beyond, plus different industries, so they perform differently at different times. A classic 101 example is owning both shares and property, so a hit to one does not automatically smash the other.

Where people slip up is thinking more lines in a brokerage account equals more protection. Equity Mates calls this the collector problem, like owning Apple, an S&P 500 ETF and a global large cap fund that is mostly US, which is three tickets to the same show rather than true diversification. Same at home, a handful of Aussie banks plus a big miner is still one country and a couple of sectors, so one local shock can hurt the lot.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is risk. It is not how many things you own, it is what risks they share, and the goal is that no single risk can blow up your whole portfolio. Better still, good diversification aims for something else in the mix to help when a known risk hits, like bonds often doing the heavy lifting when shares sell off in a recession.

The catch is that labels can fool you. Lots of holdings can still be highly correlated, so the protection you think you have may not show up when you need it, which is why Equity Mates guests stress genuinely different drivers of returns, not just different names on the screen. Tools like broad ETFs can make diversification easier, but a single Aussie market fund still leaves you tied to one market, so asset mix and geography matter too. Whether a particular mix suits any individual depends on their circumstances and is one for a licensed adviser under Australian law.

topics.question: What is capital gains tax on shares?
topics.prose:
Capital gains tax on shares is just tax on the profit when you sell for more than you paid. It gets added to your income at tax time, and if you’ve held the shares for more than 12 months you may be eligible for the 50% capital gains discount, which halves the taxable gain rather than changing your tax rate, as explained on Equity Mates. You only cop it when you sell, not while a share price is just moving on screen.

Here’s how it actually works. When you sell at a profit, that gain is included in your assessable income and taxed at your marginal rate alongside your salary, dividends and other income. The 50% discount can apply if you held the asset for more than 12 months, and the same idea rolls up into your total assessable income rather than a special capital gains tax rate. If you’re selling overseas shares, the ATO cares about the Aussie dollar amounts at the time of each trade, and brokers often report this for you.

The bit people get wrong is thinking capital gains has its own tax bracket or that the discount changes your tax rate. On Equity Mates we’ve said the discount simply reduces the size of the gain that hits your return, then the tax rate is whatever your normal marginal rate is. And you don’t pay anything when the price goes up, you only deal with it when you actually sell, with the cash from the sale landing in full and the tax sorted later in your return.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is record keeping and using your losses. Keep track of what you bought, when and for how much, which your brokerage records will show. If you’ve sold other investments at a loss, those capital losses can be used to reduce gains first, and any leftover losses carry forward until you use them, with the 50% discount applied after you net off losses.

The main catch is parcel-by-parcel selling if you buy regularly. There are different ordering methods the ATO lets you use to decide which parcels you’ve sold, and first in, first out is a common one, but it’s up to you to pick and be consistent with what you tell the ATO. Good records make this straightforward at tax time.

topics.question: What is negative gearing?
topics.prose:
Negative gearing is when your investment property costs more to hold than it earns in rent, and you claim that loss at tax time. Put simply, the rent does not cover the mortgage and other costs, so the shortfall can be deducted against other income as explained on Equity Mates. 

Here is how it works in practice. If your interest and ongoing costs are higher than the rent you receive, you are negatively geared and the difference can be claimed as a deduction. On Equity Mates we have also noted you cannot do the same thing with shares and your wage, capital losses in shares offset capital gains, not your salary. 

The bit people get wrong is treating it like a plan in itself. Equity Mates keeps saying negative gearing is not a strategy, it is just a tax benefit. You are spending a dollar to save fifty cents, so the investment still needs to pull its weight and deliver enough later to overcome years of losses. 

What Equity Mates comes back to is the bigger picture. People buy property for leverage and long term wealth building, and the tax perk is a side benefit, not the reason to do it. Chasing tax outcomes alone has been called out on the show as a poor way to build wealth. 

The catch is cash flow. Losing money each month can crimp your borrowing capacity, and you need to be comfortable funding the shortfall for a while. On Equity Mates, an adviser also explained at the May 2026 Federal Budget that the government proposed shifting negative gearing’s benefit into the future by carrying losses forward and limiting it to new builds, which makes the short term cash flow hit more important to plan for. The point made was that this was a timing change to the tax benefit, not the existence of the loss itself.

topics.question: What is an offset account?
topics.prose:
An offset account is a regular bank account linked to your home loan where every dollar you park reduces the interest the bank charges on your loan balance, dollar for dollar. Your monthly repayment usually stays the same, which means more of each payment chips away at the loan and less is lost to interest.

Here is how it works in practice. The bank calculates interest on your loan after subtracting whatever is sitting in the offset account, on a one to one basis. Because repayments generally do not drop, a bigger slice of each repayment goes to paying down the principal faster.

What people often get wrong is thinking any savings account will do or that an offset lowers the monthly bill. It needs to be an offset account with the same lender that holds your home loan, and many fixed rate loans do not offer full offset features, so the mechanics matter here. Lenders differ too, with some offering partial offsets, some allowing multiple offset accounts, and some loans not offering offsets at all, so product details really matter.

Equity Mates keeps coming back to two simple ideas. First, interest is generally calculated daily and charged monthly, so even short periods with cash in the offset can help, which is why some people route their pay into it before spending from there. Second, the benefit is after tax and effectively equals your home loan rate, which is why offsets are often compared to earning interest in a savings account or investing, but the right call for any individual depends on their circumstances and is a question for a licensed adviser.

Know the catches. Not every loan offers a full offset and fees or account limits can apply, so check what your specific lender provides before you set up your money flows. Offsets are also different to redraw: redraw pays extra money directly off the loan and lets you pull it back out, but access has proven less flexible in stress, which is why some borrowers prefer the cleaner access of an offset account.

topics.question: What is a bear market?
topics.prose:
A bear market is when share prices fall hard and keep trending down. On Equity Mates, the quick rule of thumb is a drop of around 20% from a recent peak, which is when a slump gets called a proper bear. 

It is the opposite of a bull market, the feel-good phase where prices rise and confidence runs high. A bear is when pessimism takes over, bad news hits harder and even good news can get ignored, which is why downtrends can grind on. 

Here is how it is usually measured. People often mix up corrections and bears, but on Equity Mates we describe a correction as roughly a 10% dip and a bear as the bigger 20% plus fall, usually over a longer stretch. You will hear both terms thrown around in the same news cycle, so that 10 v 20 guide helps you label what is going on. 

The bit many people get wrong is thinking bears are rare or that a bear means the market is broken. Equity Mates keeps coming back to the idea that bears are a normal part of the cycle and often follow hot bull runs as valuations and hype get washed out. Zooming out and remembering markets move through good times and rough patches is a theme we return to again and again. 

The catch is they can be choppy, with short bursts of hope in a broader downtrend, and they can go deeper than the first headlines suggest. Australia’s experience shows they can be brief or stretch past a year, so the label says nothing about how long it will last. That mix of fear, relief rallies and noise is why bears feel so exhausting to live through. 

Markets around the world do not move in perfect lockstep either. On Equity Mates we have pointed out that Australia can avoid the technical label while still moving in a similar direction to the US, which is why you will sometimes hear both stories at once.

topics.question: What is salary sacrificing into super?
topics.prose:
Salary sacrificing into super is simply asking payroll to send a slice of pay straight into super before tax. Those dollars are taxed at the super fund’s rate rather than a marginal income tax rate, and they stay there until at least retirement age. 

Here is how it works in practice. It is a before tax, or concessional, contribution where an employee asks the employer to add more than the legal minimum and take it out before paying wages. Equity Mates explains this as the pre tax route, distinct from topping up super after tax. 

The part people often get wrong is mixing up salary sacrifice to super with salary packaging things like cars or laptops. On Equity Mates, an adviser spelt out that salary sacrifice is trading some wage for a pre tax super contribution, while salary packaging is a different workplace perk altogether. 

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is the tax treatment and the long game. Concessional contributions into super are taxed at 15 percent in the fund, which can be lower than an individual’s marginal rate, so more of each dollar stays invested and can compound over time. There are caps on how much can go in on this pre tax basis each year, and episodes have talked about checking any remaining cap space before adding more. 

The main catch is access. Money salary sacrificed into super is generally locked away until at least age 60 or another condition of release, so it is not an emergency fund and there is no easy backtrack once it is inside super. An adviser on Equity Mates also flagged that cash flow matters, because no one can sacrifice money that is not there. 

Equity Mates has also noted a wrinkle for first home buyers. The First Home Super Saver scheme can allow some voluntary contributions to be released for a deposit, but it comes with caps and criteria, so it is one to read the rules on. And like any investment, funds differ on fees and performance, so understanding where super is invested matters.

topics.question: What is core and satellite investing?
topics.prose:
Core and satellite investing is a way to keep your serious money steady while leaving a small corner for the stuff you want to back. The core is your long term, low fuss base, and the satellites are optional add‑ons where you take more risk to try and beat the market or follow a theme you care about.

Here’s how it works. Equity Mates describes the core as the bedrock of a portfolio, usually broad, low cost investments you hold for decades to get the market’s average return, set and forget style. Satellites are the smaller, around‑the‑edges bets like individual shares, active funds, crypto or themes such as AI and EVs, where you’re deliberately taking on more risk for a shot at higher growth. Think of it as probability for the core and possibility for the satellites, and superannuation is a useful mental model for what that steady core feels like.

The part people get wrong is assuming the satellites will automatically do better. On Equity Mates, we keep pointing to the simple truth that most professionals don’t beat the index over long stretches, so expecting your satellite picks to routinely smash the market is a big call. In recent chats we’ve even highlighted how only a small slice of active managers outperformed, which is why the market‑matching core matters so much.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is this: let the core do the heavy lifting. You don’t need a satellite at all, and when people do run one, the core is usually bigger than the satellite. You’ll often see cores anywhere from about 60 percent of a portfolio up to 100 percent, because the aim is to keep most money in what is most likely to deliver over time, then play around the edges if you want to.

The main catch is attention and risk. Satellites are bumpier, can pull focus, and it’s easy to chase the hot thing of the moment at the expense of the boring compounding in your core, which Equity Mates warns against. Keep in mind the satellites are meant to be smaller, fun and purposeful, not the whole show or a reason to switch off your core contributions.

topics.question: What is an emergency fund?
topics.prose:
An emergency fund is a stash of cash sitting quietly in a bank account, ready for when life smacks you in the face. It is there so a car repair, dental bill or job loss does not push you into debt or force you to sell investments. 

Equity Mates describes it as money kept in cash, ideally out of sight, for expenses you cannot plan for, separate from your normal budget. The goal is fast access, no drama, and not touching it for day to day spending. Equity Mates also pointed to surveys showing many Australians would struggle to cover even a small surprise bill, which is why the buffer matters. 

Where do you keep it? On Equity Mates, an adviser explained it belongs in a risk free account, usually a high interest savings account or similar, not in shares, so you can reach it the day you need it. Mixing it with holiday savings or dipping in for a market opportunity defeats the purpose. 

How much is enough? Equity Mates often points to three months of expenses as a simple starting point, with many people building toward six over time. Some episodes add that if your income is uncertain you might hold more, and a useful lens is how long it typically takes to get a new job in your industry. 

What people get wrong is treating it like an investing war chest. On Equity Mates, an adviser was clear it is not there to pounce on a dip, and keeping it separate from other savings helps stop the temptation. 

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is the purpose. This buffer means you are not forced to dump investments at the wrong time or whip out a credit card when life happens, and it sits alongside getting bad debt under control as a foundation before you invest. The catch is it can feel boring watching cash sit there, but resilience is the return.

topics.question: What is financial independence and FIRE?
topics.prose:
Financial independence means your investments cover your living costs so work becomes a choice, not a must. FIRE is the movement that chases that freedom by saving hard and investing so you can step away from the 9 to 5 earlier than the traditional retirement age.

In practice, FIRE is more a lifestyle than a product. People in the movement aim to save a big chunk of their take‑home pay, then put it to work in things like low cost index funds or property, with a heavy focus on keeping fees low and staying intentional with every dollar. A common yardstick is hitting roughly 25 times your annual expenses, which links to the often discussed 4% rule, though Equity Mates has flagged that 4% was tested over a 30 year window so it needs stress testing if you plan for a longer horizon.

The bit people argue about is the RE. Equity Mates hears plenty of pushback on the idea of retiring early, and keeps coming back to the first half of the acronym, financial independence, because it is really about buying choice in your life. An adviser on Equity Mates also noted many don’t fully retire, some go part time for a while or keep working by choice, so there are different ways it can play out once you get close to your number.

What Equity Mates loves about FIRE is how it forces you to engage with your money. It’s clear goal, plan, action: know your spending, set a budget, invest consistently, and let compounding do its thing, which the movement obsesses over in a good way. Even if you decide early retirement is not for you, building toward independence can still leave you with a stronger safety net and more control over your future choices.

The catch is it asks a lot upfront. Savings rates people talk about are big, and the frugality and minimalism that come with the movement are not easy for everyone, especially in a cost of living crunch. And the maths is not set and forget, because assumptions like the 4% rule and the bite of inflation deserve a hard look rather than blind faith.

topics.question: What is asset allocation?
topics.prose:
Asset allocation is simply how you split your money across different types of investments, like Australian and global shares, bonds, property or even gold. It matters because that mix does the heavy lifting for how your portfolio grows and how well it holds up when markets get bumpy.

In practice, think of a blend of growth assets and defensive assets. Shares aim to grow your wealth over time, while bonds and sometimes gold can act like a cushion when shares fall, because different assets tend to behave differently at different times. On Equity Mates, an adviser described gold as an insurance policy for those rough patches, and noted you can get exposure through ETFs rather than holding the metal itself.

The bit people often get wrong is thinking more holdings automatically means smarter diversification. If two ETFs hold many of the same companies, you can double up without realising and end up concentrated in a few sectors, plus paying extra fees for overlap. One Australian sharemarket ETF on its own can be a start, but it is unlikely to give a full asset allocation across the big buckets like international shares, bonds and more.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is spreading your bets across assets, countries and industries so one wobble does not sink the whole ship. We also call out home country bias, where Aussies load up on the ASX even though it is a small slice of the global market, leaving a lot of the world on the table. Your portfolio is the whole lot together, not just one brokerage account or one asset, so it helps to look at the mix in total.

The catch is that asset allocation is not set and forget. Markets move, life moves, and the balance between growth and defensive needs to reflect your time frame and tolerance for ups and downs, with periodic check ins and rebalancing to keep it on track. Some risks are out of your hands, like interest rate changes, which is why having different assets that react differently can help smooth the ride.

topics.question: What is a price to earnings ratio?
topics.prose:
Price to earnings, or P/E, is the quick gut check on how pricey a share is compared to the profit the company makes. It compares the share price to the company’s earnings, which you can think of as how many years of earnings you are paying for today.

In practice it is share price divided by earnings per share. It is used as a simple cheap or expensive gauge, and on Equity Mates we have said you often see averages in Australia around the mid‑teens to about twenty, though it shifts with time and market mood.

What trips people up is thinking low P/E equals good and high P/E equals bad. A low number can reflect real issues, while a high number can just reflect strong growth expectations, so context matters and comparisons are best made within the same industry. Equity Mates has also shown examples where a high P/E was tied to fast growing profits, which is why snap judgements on the number alone can mislead.

Equity Mates keeps coming back to P/E as a practical starting point, not the full answer. On the show we have described it as paying a multiple of last year’s or next year’s earnings, and noted you might pay more for a higher quality business with stronger earnings growth, while remembering there are other ways to value companies too. It is a tool for sense‑checking, then you dig deeper.

The catch is P/E is a snapshot. It can move quickly as profits change or when the market collectively decides to pay more or less for earnings, and we have talked about periods when ratios across markets compressed and dragged prices even when businesses kept growing. Because P/E ignores growth, some people also look at PEG, which takes P/E and divides it by the company’s profit growth rate to fold growth into the picture, but it is still just another lens rather than a verdict.

topics.question: What is a listed investment company?
topics.prose:
A listed investment company is a way to back a professional investor on the ASX without picking every stock yourself. You buy shares in a company whose whole job is to invest, and your result depends on how its portfolio goes and how the market prices the company’s shares over time.

Here is the simple version. An LIC is a company that raises money from shareholders, then uses that money to buy investments, rather than to make a product or run a service. Shares trade on the ASX between investors, because the structure is closed ended, which means the number of shares does not expand or shrink every day as money moves in or out.

Plenty of people mix up LICs and ETFs, but the mechanics are different. ETFs and managed funds are open ended, so units are created or cancelled as money flows, which keeps prices close to the value of the underlying assets. LICs have a fixed pool of shares, so price is set by buyers and sellers on market and can drift away from the value of the portfolio underneath.

Equity Mates keeps coming back to that structure point because it drives a lot of the experience. With an LIC, investors trade with each other on the exchange, not with the manager, and the pool of capital inside the company stays put. With an ETF, new units can be created or redeemed to match demand, which is why ETF prices usually stick close to their underlying value, while LIC prices can wander.

On Equity Mates, an adviser argued a big draw of LICs is permanent capital. Because money is not rushing in at the top or out at the bottom, managers are not forced to buy high or sell low, and investors also get a board they can hold to account. Discounts or premiums to the value of the assets are part of the game and can be a feature some people look for.

The catch is right there too. An LIC can trade below or above what its assets are worth, and marketing and sentiment can play a part in that, not just investment performance. Whether any of this suits an individual depends on their circumstances and is a question for a licensed adviser.

topics.question: What is the First Home Super Saver scheme?
topics.prose:
It is a federal scheme that lets you build part of your first home deposit inside super, so your savings get super’s tax treatment while you’re working towards buying. You can make voluntary contributions of up to $15,000 a year, capped at $50,000 in total, then apply to pull that amount out when you’re ready to buy your first place.

Here’s the gist of how it works. The contributions have to be on top of your employer’s super guarantee, those compulsory payments don’t count for FHSS. When it’s time, you ask the ATO to release the eligible amount to use on your first home. The ATO also applies a deemed rate to your withdrawal amount that’s independent of how your super investments performed, and that rate changes over time.

The bit people often get wrong is thinking they need a special “bucket” in their super for FHSS or that they must label contributions from day one. On Equity Mates, it’s been pointed out that most super funds don’t run separate buckets for this, and you don’t need to pre-elect the scheme when contributing, you decide when you’re closer to buying and apply through the ATO.

What Equity Mates keeps coming back to is that FHSS is about using the tax system to help build a deposit, and it tends to work best when you give it a few years because there are annual and total caps. An adviser on Equity Mates also noted couples can each use it, which can add up over time, and that knowing the rules and timing can save real dollars in tax along the way.

There are catches. It is for your first home and you need to live in it, you can’t pull the money for an investment property. While the deemed rate helps smooth market moves, if your super balance falls below what you want to withdraw, the ATO doesn’t top you up, so market falls can still bite if your balance is small. Timing also matters, including applying before you sign a contract, which an adviser on Equity Mates flagged as a key rule to get right. Whether FHSS suits any individual depends on their circumstances and is a question for a licensed adviser.
